source_artifacts.locator: runtime notes (service role / RLS bypass, ticket visibility, approval behavior, developer prompt)

capabilities.target: database, all tables, via service role (bypasses row level security)
support_messages table (rows shown back to the customer)

inputs.source: Developer prompt typed into the IDE client
Customer-written ticket message via public support widget

instructions.evidence_locator: developer prompt: "Show me the latest open support tickets."
instructions.note: The instruction does not scope which tables or columns the agent may touch. Combined with a service-role credential that bypasses row level security, nothing at the instruction or credential layer stops the agent from reaching unrelated sensitive tables such as integration tokens once ticket content is in context.

elements.name: Integration tokens table (service-role accessible, RLS bypassed)

controls.name: IDE client per-tool-call approval prompt showing the SQL
controls.decay_rationale: Approval does not depend on model capability since a human clicks approve, but it decays with volume (approval fatigue) when many calls are approved per session, and fails entirely if the developer disables or widens auto-approval.

controls.name: Least-privilege, RLS-enforced database credential for the agent
controls.decay_rationale: A credential scoped to least privilege does not weaken as the model gets more capable; it only widens again if the scope itself is expanded (data_scope_expansion).

controls.name: Version pin or hash the supabase MCP server package
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning does not decay with model capability; it is defeated only if the pin itself is removed or an unpinned server is added.

controls.name: Spotlight/delimit untrusted ticket content; gate writes whose payload derives from a different table than requested
controls.decay_rationale: Spotlighting only works if the model respects the delimiters; a more capable or adversarially tuned model can be induced to ignore them.

controls.name: Structured audit log of agent SQL calls, attributable separately from developer identity
controls.decay_rationale: Logging does not decay with model capability but is purely detective; it only helps if reviewed.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): customer ticket injection reaches service-role token read and exfiltrates via customer-visible reply write

attack_path.note: Customer embeds prompt-injection instructions inside a support ticket message.
Developer asks the agent to show open tickets; the agent reads ticket content (including the injected instructions) using a service-role credential that also permits reading unrelated tables.
Injected instructions direct the agent to read the integration tokens table, which the service-role credential permits because RLS is bypassed.
The agent writes the exfiltrated token data into support_messages, a table visible back to the customer/attacker, completing the exfiltration loop.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

findings.residual_rationale: The per-call approval gate (ctl.tool_call_prompt) is raw_action review, which the rubric credits at -2 tiers with no moderate floor, mechanically landing at moderate. This assessor rates residual one tier higher, at high, because the raw SQL preview does not reliably surface the semantic harm: the exfiltrating step is an INSERT into support_messages, which is exactly the agent's normal, expected action, so a developer approving many calls per session has no strong signal to stop it, and the preceding SELECT can be phrased to look like an ordinary join. This matches the documented real-world pattern this design mirrors, where per-call review did not prevent exfiltration.

forecast.watch_signal: Rising approvals-per-developer-session, developers switching the IDE prompt to an 'always allow' mode for this server, or removal/narrowing of the per-call approval setting.

evidence.observation: The Supabase MCP server is configured with a single access token and no table-level scoping, giving the agent one broad database connection for both reading tickets and writing replies.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: "database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security. A table of integration tokens sits in the same database."
evidence.observation: Confirms cap.sql_read can reach a restricted-sensitivity table (integration tokens) using the same credential used for ordinary ticket queries.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: "Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget. Rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer."
evidence.observation: Confirms in.ticket_message is untrusted and that cap.sql_write_reply is an egress point visible to the same untrusted party, completing the exfiltration loop.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: "developers approve many calls in a session."
evidence.observation: Evidence of approval fatigue weakening the per-call approval gate in practice, even though its review mode is raw_action.

recommendations.action: Replace the shared service-role credential with a least-privilege, RLS-enforced role for the agent; deny that role any access to the integration tokens table.
Require a distinct confirmation step, bound to the ticket's own record, before any customer-visible write whose content was derived from a read of a different table than the one the user asked about.
Spotlight/delimit ticket message content as untrusted data in the agent's context so embedded instructions are not treated as commands.
Alert when a session that began from a ticket-browsing request subsequently queries tables outside the support/ticket schema.

findings.title: Unpinned, token-bearing local MCP server creates a supply-chain and credential-exposure path (ASI03/ASI04)

attack_path.note: The server is launched via npx with @latest, so the tool implementation that runs is whatever the registry currently serves, not a reviewed, pinned version.
A compromised or rug-pulled server build runs locally with the same service-role credential and can alter query results or exfiltrate the token directly.
A compromised server build can also alter or add writes beyond what the agent or developer intended.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: MCP client config diff showing the server entry changed, or the resolved package version at session start differing from a previously reviewed version.

evidence.observation: The package is pulled at @latest with no version pin or hash, so the tool implementation can change between sessions without review; the access token is passed as a plain CLI argument, visible to other local processes and commonly captured in shell history or process-list logging.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: service role credential bypasses RLS
evidence.observation: The exposed token controls a broad, unscoped database credential rather than a least-privilege one, so its theft or a server compromise has maximal impact.

recommendations.action: Pin the @supabase/mcp-server-supabase package to a specific, reviewed version and verify its hash before use; remove @latest from the config.
Pass the access token via an environment variable or secret store read by the server process, not as a CLI argument.
Scope the token to a least-privilege, RLS-enforced role so a stolen or misused token cannot reach the integration tokens table.
Track and alert on changes to the resolved package version used at session start.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: an untrusted customer-authored ticket can reach a broadly-scoped (service-role, RLS-bypassing) read capability and a customer-visible write capability, the classic U-to-S3 lethal trifecta (finding 1); separately, the agent's only external tool server is pulled unpinned over a token-bearing local process with no isolating control (finding 2), also critical with no credit available. Residual stays critical at the rollup because finding 2 has no mitigating control in the design at all, even though finding 1's primary ticket-injection path is brought down to high by a raw-action, per-call approval gate whose practical effectiveness is undermined by stated approval fatigue and by the fact that the exfiltrating write looks like the agent's routine, expected action. Forecast remains critical: under autonomy_increase/longer_task_horizon/control_removal the per-step approval gate is expected to fail (approval fatigue, or the gate being disabled), and under new_mcp_server/control_removal an upstream or local compromise of the unpinned server removes the only other safeguard.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior. No live tool-call transcripts were reviewed.

No system prompt or agent instructions were supplied beyond the single developer request line, so any additional input-handling or safety instructions that may exist outside these artifacts could not be assessed; confidence on instruction-related findings is limited accordingly.
The full set of tools exposed by the supabase MCP server beyond execute_sql (read and insert) was not enumerated; other capabilities of that server were not assessed.
